newsitem.title: CHINA: New HK govt needs elections to avert legal crisis.
newsitem.headline: New HK govt needs elections to avert legal crisis.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa should call legislative elections in the former British colony as rapidly as possible or face a constitutional crisis, legal experts said on Friday.
At issue is the legality of an unelected legislature which Beijing has appointed to make laws for Chinese-ruled Hong Kong until new elections are held -- possibly next May.
The experts said Tung, who indicated after taking office this week that legislative elections would take place in the second quarter of 1998, should not wait that long.

After 156 years of British control, the colony reverted to China as a quasi-autonomous region last Monday night, with a promise from Beijing that its capitalist lifestyle will remain unchanged and it will enjoy considerable autonomy under a "one country two systems" policy.
The first alarm bell rang out on Thursday, the first working day in the fledgling Special Administrative Region (SAR).
During the first case tried in the new-born Hong Kong, barrister Paul Harris, a prominent human rights advocate, stood up and told the judge the legal system was unconstitutional.
"I said I appeared for my client on the basis of the doctrine of necessity, which required the courts to continue to operate even if there is a constitutional vacuum," Harris told Reuters.
He said a constitutional vacuum existed because the Provisional Legislature was not properly elected, as required by the Basic Law, Hong Kong's new Chinese-penned constitution.
"The Basic Law makes quite detailed provisions for the first Legislative Council of the Hong Kong SAR.
"It's to be an elected body, it's to have various members elected in various different ways and it's very similar to the last colonial legislature," Harris said.
"There is absolutely no mention (in the Basic Law) of a provisional legislature and no mention of legislation by some body that isn't elected," Harris said.
Other academics echoed his view on the assembly's authority to pass laws, and said a possible solution would be for Tung to go for early elections.

"This election will be quite important. At this time we will be able to see if the promise of one country two systems could be fulfilled, it's the first real test," said Michel Bonnin, director of the French Centre on Contemporary China.
The legal vacuum was a bad beginning for the new government, legal experts said. But not all was lost.
Elections would allow laws passed by the interim body to be approved by the elected body, averting a crisis.
"Now China has complete control of the government here and the political system. They have nominated the people who selected Tung Chee-hwa, so they have control of the executive power," Bonnin said.

"For legislative power, they have indirectly nominated people in the Provisional Legislature, so nothing seems to be out of their control," he said, but he noted that China might cleverly avoid abusing this power.
Provisional Legislature president Rita Fan has said the council is protected by the umbrella of China's legal system, Provisional Legislature spokesman Simon Wong noted.
"So there is no question about its legality, if there is any legal challenge, she will deal with it in accordance with legal procedures of the Hong Kong SAR," said Wong.

According to visiting French international law specialist Ghislaine Chabanol, Britain and China have different interpretations of the Basic Law, notably on the issue of democratic electoral reforms introduced by last colonial governor Chris Patten.

China said the legislature elected under Patten's new rules in 1995 was incompatible with the letter and the spirit of the Basic Law. As promised, Beijing dissolved it at the stroke of midnight on Monday and put the nominated chamber in its place. Britain denounced the move as unconstitutional.

"A final assessment of the Provisional Legislature's legality would partly depend on the speed with which elections to the first (post-handover) legislative council were organised," said Chabanol, a visiting scholar at Hong Kong University.
"The best way would be if any kind of law passed by the Provisional Legislature would get a final ratification by the first elected legislature," she added.
